items: Fall Chinook fishing has been slow to fair in the North Coast rivers. The Trask and Wilson Rivers have been the biggest producers, but there are fish being caught in the Nestucca, Little Nestucca, Three Rivers, Kilchis, Nehalem, and Necanicum Rivers as well. Fishing has really slowed down in the bays with very few fish being harvested.
The Trask River, North Fork Nehalem River, and Lower Columbia Tributaries have hatchery coho salmon runs and a few fish are being caught though, overall, fishing has been slow.
The Kilchis and Miami Rivers closed to catch and release fishing for chum on November 16. They are still open for fall Chinook fishing but targeting chum is prohibited.
Hebo Lake and Town Lake were stocked with trophy trout a couple weeks ago. This was an unscheduled stocking. These are big trout that are fun to catch!

Fall Chinook fishing has been slow in the Siletz, Alsea, Siuslaw, Yaquina and Salmon rivers. This much needed rain should get some fish moving throughout the basins. As a reminder, Chinook are spawning in many systems and anglers are asked to be mindful of fish on redds. Refer to Fall Coastal Salmon Management for more information on season outlines and bag limits.
Wild coho retention has closed in the Siletz, Yaquina and Siuslaw rivers for the year.
Siltcoos and Tahkenitch lakes are open for wild coho retention. Dedicated anglers are landing a few coho in Siltcoos Lake. The rain should raise the creeks and bring more fish into the lakes.
Reminder to purchase required 2027 validation and harvest tag for winter steelhead in the Rogue Basin or on the South Coast, good through Dec 1 through April 30, 2027.
Empire, Saunders, and Butterfield Lakes were stocked recently with legal trout. Bradley Lake and Powers ponds were stocked the week of November 15.
Diamond Lake is still producing some nice rainbows, along with catch and release brown and tiger trout. Although the forecast has some cold wet weather for the weekend.

Recent rains have kick started fall chinook fishing in the Elk and Sixes Rivers. As always anglers will want to watch the weather and try and fish as rivers flows are dropping after a rain event. This is a good time of year to visit Elk River Hatchery with fall chinook returning to the hatchery on a daily basis.
Due to continuing dry conditions, Junction City Pond will not be stocked until the first week of December to allow for more rain to fill the pond.
Timber Linn in Albany and Walter Wirth Lake and Turner Lake in Salem are in good shape and have been stocked recently.
Following trophy trout stockings, the Fall River has been fishing exceptionally well.
Reports of consistent trout fishing on the lower Deschutes around the Trout Creek area.

Road closures and snow have limited access to many Central Zone lakes; however, lower elevation waterbodies including Lake Billy Chinook, Haystack Reservoir, and Ochoco Reservoir are good options during the winter months.

Tiger Muskies are hungry and aggressive at Phillips Reservoir. Try your luck before winter sets in. Water temperature is prime right now in the low 50°F. Fishing should remain hot until water temps drop below 45°F. As a bonus, the low water levels will concentrate fish and may make catching fish easier.

The Umatilla River should provide good coho fishing opportunity through the end of November. Steelhead are also disbursed throughout the river, but the highest concentrations are still in the lower portion.

Anglers are catching steelhead in both the Grande Ronde and Imnaha Rivers. Focus lower on both rivers this time of year. Fishing jigs under bobbers has been effective for catching late fall steelhead.

Malheur Reservoir – great for Rainbow Trout from 10-22". Common sizes are 12-16" but we captured fish up to 22" in our sampling this week. We also fly-fished it in the evening and morning and had catches of 10+ trout/hr. We saw people having success trolling and bank fishing with bait as well. Water temperatures were in the mid 50's. You can launch a boat from the boat ramp. Water is up to the old school bus. If you know you know.

Yellowjacket Reservoir – Great fishing without a crowd! We sampled last week and found fish from 8-18" with a common size of 12-15". We fished leech patterns under an indicator midday and had non-stop action. Water temperatures are in the mid-50's here, too.
Many streams are closed to protect spawning Redband Trout and Chinook Salmon in the Klamath Basin. Your best bets are Klamath Lake and Klamath River below Keno Dam for Redband Trout.
Yellow perch angling still might be good in Lake of the Woods, Gerber Reservoir and Upper Klamath Lake near Rocky Point.
Big Brown Trout are cruising the shoreline at Miller Lake.
Crappie angling has been excellent at Dog Lake recently.

Salmon, steelhead, and shad. The lower Columbia creel program has ended for the year and will resume in February 2027. The creel program above Bonneville will continue for a couple more weeks.
Salmon, steelhead, and shad. Bonneville Dam to McNary Dam: Weekly checking showed three coho and one Chinook released for eight boats (17 anglers).
Bonneville Dam to McNary Dam: Weekly checking showed two sublegal, six legal sized and 10 over-legal sized white sturgeon released for four boats (13 anglers).
Walleye. Bonneville Dam to McNary Dam: Weekly checking showed no catch for six boats (15 anglers).

Marine fishing. Lingcod and many other bottomfish species are available year-round to shore anglers fishing in rocky areas. A common setup for lingcod is a jig head with a rubber swim bait – it's simple but effective. Also pack a measuring device for lingcod: the minimum legal size is 22 inches.

Marine fishing. Surfperch are available in the surf year-round along sandy beaches and rocky shores, with the best fishing (and safest fishing) occurring when swells are small. Find surfperch and other learn to fish workshops and events here .

Marine fishing. When fishing from shore or inside estuaries and bays, it is important to check the tide. Many fish that swim into estuaries and bays, including salmon, surfperch, and Pacific herring, tend to come in with the tide. Catch of these species is more likely to occur closer to slack tide. Additionally, the accessibility of some areas can be completely dependent on the tide. Do not allow the incoming tide to become a safety issue.
